title: Process vs Thread — memory space, stack, overhead
shortTitle: Process vs Thread — memory space, stack, overhead

s1_definition.profdef: A **process** is an independent running program with its own ISOLATED memory space (heap, code segment, data segment). Each process gets its own address space from the OS. If one process crashes, others continue running. Communication between processes requires IPC (Inter-Process Communication) — sockets, pipes, shared memory — which is relatively expensive. A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution WITHIN a process. All threads in a process SHARE the same heap memory, but each thread has its OWN stack (local variables, method calls). Threads are cheaper to create (~1MB stack, ~1ms) vs processes (~100ms). The trade-off: shared memory enables fast communication but requires SYNCHRONIZATION to prevent data corruption.
s1_definition.analogy: A **process** is a separate bank BRANCH — own building, own vault, own staff. If one branch burns down, other branches continue operating. Communication between branches: slow mail/courier (IPC). A **thread** is an employee WITHIN one branch. All employees share the same vault (heap memory) and can access any drawer. But if two employees try to update the SAME account register simultaneously without coordinating (synchronization), the register gets corrupted. Each employee has their own desk with personal notes (own stack).
s1_definition.oneliner: Process = own memory, isolated, heavy, crash-safe. Thread = shared heap, own stack, lightweight, needs synchronization. Threads share data fast but must coordinate access.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A **process** is an independent running program with its own ISOLATED memory space (heap, code segment, data segment). Each process gets its own address space from the OS. If one process crashes, others continue running. Communication between processes requires IPC (Inter-Process Communication) — sockets, pipes, shared memory — which is relatively expensive. A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution WITHIN a process. All threads in a process SHARE the same heap memory, but each thread has its OWN stack (local variables, method calls). Threads are cheaper to create (~1MB stack, ~1ms) vs processes (~100ms). The trade-off: shared memory enables fast communication but requires SYNCHRONIZATION to prevent data corruption.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A **process** is a separate bank BRANCH — own building, own vault, own staff. If one branch burns down, other branches continue operating. Communication between branches: slow mail/courier (IPC). A **thread** is an employee WITHIN one branch. All employees share the same vault (heap memory) and can access any drawer. But if two employees try to update the SAME account register simultaneously without coordinating (synchronization), the register gets corrupted. Each employee has their own desk with personal notes (own stack).

**One line to remember:** Process = own memory, isolated, heavy, crash-safe. Thread = shared heap, own stack, lightweight, needs synchronization. Threads share data fast but must coordinate access.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's trading platform needs to handle 10,000 concurrent trade orders per second.** Using separate processes for each order: 10,000 processes × 100MB = 1TB RAM — impossible. Fix: ONE process (JVM) with 200 threads. Each thread handles one trade order. All threads share the order book (heap memory). Thread creation: ~1ms each. Communication: direct shared memory access (nanoseconds). But: shared order book needs synchronization — two threads can't modify the same order simultaneously.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** JVM process starts — OS allocates memory (heap + metaspace). One main thread created.

**Step 2.** Main thread creates 10 worker threads. Each thread gets its own stack (~1MB). All share the same heap.

**Step 3.** All 10 threads increment a shared AtomicInteger. Each thread reads the counter, atomically increments, writes back. No race condition because AtomicInteger uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

**Step 4.** Without AtomicInteger: two threads read balance=100000 simultaneously, both compute 99000, both write 99000. One decrement LOST. With AtomicInteger: CAS ensures only one thread's write succeeds; the other retries.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ PROCESS vs THREAD ═══

  Process 1 (Trading API)              Process 2 (Settlement Service)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ JVM Heap (shared)       │          │ JVM Heap (separate!)    │
  │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐    │          │ ┌───────┐              │
  │ │Thread1│ │Thread2│ ...│          │ │Thread1│ ...           │
  │ │Stack  │ │Stack  │    │          │ │Stack  │              │
  │ └───────┘ └───────┘    │    IPC   │ └───────┘              │
  │ Shared: orderBook,     │◄────────►│ Shared: settlements    │
  │   balanceCache          │ (slow!)  │                        │
  └─────────────────────────┘          └─────────────────────────┘

  Within ONE process:
  Thread-1 stack: [localVar=100, methodFrame...]
  Thread-2 stack: [localVar=200, methodFrame...]
  SHARED heap:    [balance=100000, orderBook, cache]
  → Fast communication (shared memory)
  → Needs synchronization (race conditions!)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Trading Platform Process/Thread Architecture ═══

  ┌──────────────┐    REST    ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ Trading UI   │───────────→│  Trading API (Process 1)   │
  └──────────────┘            │  200 threads (thread pool)  │

                              └──────────┬─────────────────┘
                                         │ Kafka (IPC)
                              ┌──────────▼─────────────────┐
                              │  Settlement (Process 2)     │
                              │  50 threads                  │
                              │  Shared: SettlementLedger   │
                              └──────────┬─────────────────┘

                              ┌──────────▼─────────────────┐
                              │  PostgreSQL (Process 3)     │

  Processes: isolated, communicate via Kafka/REST (slow but safe)
  Threads within process: shared heap (fast but needs sync)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread vs Process Memory Model ═══

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           JVM Process                    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  HEAP (shared by ALL threads):          │
  │    - orderBook: ConcurrentHashMap       │
  │    - balanceCache: AtomicInteger[]      │
  │    - tradeQueue: LinkedBlockingQueue    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  METASPACE: loaded classes, method code │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐            │
  │  │ Thread-1 │  │ Thread-2 │  ...       │
  │  │ Stack:   │  │ Stack:   │            │
  │  │ -localAmt│  │ -localAmt│  (separate)│
  │  │ -frame[] │  │ -frame[] │            │
  │  │ PC, SP   │  │ PC, SP   │            │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Race condition: Thread-1 reads balance(100K), Thread-2 reads balance(100K)
  Both compute 100K-50K=50K, both write 50K. Expected 0. Got 50K. LOST UPDATE!
  Fix: AtomicInteger.addAndGet(-50000) → CAS → only one succeeds, other retries.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A process is an independent program with its own memory space — heap, code, data segment — fully isolated from other processes. If one process crashes, others survive. Communication between processes requires IPC (sockets, pipes, Kafka) which is relatively slow. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process — all threads share the same heap but each has its own stack. Thread creation is fast (~1ms, ~1MB stack) vs process creation (~100ms, ~100MB).

The trade-off: threads share memory so they can communicate instantly (nanoseconds) by reading/writing shared objects, but this requires synchronization (synchronized, Lock, Atomic classes) to prevent race conditions. Without synchronization, two threads reading and modifying the same balance simultaneously can lose updates — debiting Rs.50,000 twice but the balance only reflects one debit. In banking: one JVM process with 200 threads handles 10K trade orders/sec. Threads share the order book (ConcurrentHashMap), balance cache (AtomicInteger), and trade queue (LinkedBlockingQueue). Separate processes (via Kafka) for settlement and notification — isolated, crash-safe.
